entries.text: A modern formatting library & 10;& 10; & 10; Safety & 10; & 10; Inspired by Python's formatting facility, {fmt} provides a safe replacement& 10; for the printf family of functions. Errors in format strings,& 10; which are a common source of vulnerabilities in C, are reported at& 10; compile time . For example:& 10;& 10; fmt::format("{:d}", "I am not a number"); & 10;& 10; will give a compile-time error because d is not a valid& 10; format specifier for strings. APIs like & 10; fmt::format prevent buffer overflow errors via& 10; automatic memory management.& 10; & 10; → Learn more & 10; & 10;& 10; & 10; Extensibility & 10; & 10; Formatting of most standard types , including all containers, dates,& 10; and times is supported out-of-the-box . For example:& 10;& 10; fmt::print("{}", std::vector{1, 2, 3}); & 10;& 10; prints the vector in a JSON-like format:& 10;& 10; [1, 2, 3] & 10;& 10; You can make your own types formattable and even make compile-time& 10; checks work for them.& 10; & 10; → Learn more & 10; & 10;& 10; & 10; Performance & 10; & 10; {fmt} can be anywhere from tens of percent to 20-30 times faster than& 10; iostreams and sprintf , especially for numeric formatting.& 10;& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;& 10; The library minimizes dynamic memory allocations and can optionally& 10; compile format strings to optimal code.& 10; & 10; & 10;& 10; & 10; Unicode support & 10; & 10; {fmt} provides portable Unicode support on major operating systems& 10; with UTF-8 and char strings. For example:& 10;& 10; fmt::print("Слава Україні!"); & 10;& 10; will be printed correctly on Linux, macOS, and even Windows console,& 10; irrespective of the codepages.& 10; & 10; & 10; The default is locale-independent , but you can opt into localized& 10; formatting and {fmt} makes it work with Unicode, addressing issues in the& 10; standard library.& 10; & 10; & 10;& 10; & 10; Fast compilation & 10; & 10; The library makes extensive use of type erasure to achieve fast& 10; compilation. fmt/base.h provides a subset of the API with& 10; minimal include dependencies and enough functionality to replace& 10; all uses of printf .& 10; & 10; & 10; Code using {fmt} is usually several times faster to compile than the& 10; equivalent iostreams code, and while printf compiles faster& 10; still, the gap is narrowing.& 10; & 10; & 10;→ Learn more & 10; & 10;& 10; & 10; Small binary footprint & 10; & 10; Type erasure is also used to prevent template bloat, resulting in compact& 10; per-call binary code . For example, a call to fmt::print with& 10; a single argument is just a few& 10; instructions , comparable to printf despite adding& 10; runtime safety, and much smaller than the equivalent iostreams code.& 10; & 10; & 10; The library itself has small binary footprint and some components such as& 10; floating-point formatting can be disabled to make it even smaller for& 10; resource-constrained devices.& 10; & 10; & 10;& 10; & 10; Portability & 10; & 10; {fmt} has a small self-contained codebase with the core consisting of& 10; just three headers and no external dependencies.& 10; & 10; & 10; The library is highly portable and requires only a minimal subset of& 10; C++11 features which are available in GCC 4.9, Clang 3.6, MSVC 19.10& 10; (2017) and later. Newer compiler and standard library features are used& 10; if available, and enable additional functionality.& 10; & 10; & 10; Where possible, the output of formatting functions is consistent across& 10; platforms .& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;& 10; & 10; Open source & 10; & 10; {fmt} is in the top hundred open-source C++ libraries on GitHub and has& 10; hundreds of& 10; all-time contributors .& 10; & 10; & 10; The library is distributed under a permissive MIT& 10; license and is& 10; relied upon by many open-source projects , including Blender, PyTorch,& 10; Apple's FoundationDB, Windows Terminal, MongoDB, and others.& 10; & 10; & 10;& 10;

entries.title: Get Started
entries.text: Get Started Compile and run {fmt} examples online with Compiler Explorer. {fmt} is compatible with any build system. The next section describes its usage with CMake, while the Build Systems section covers the rest. CMake {fmt} provides three CMake targets: fmt::fmt for the standard compiled library, fmt::fmt-module for the C++ module library and fmt::fmt-header-only for the header-only library. It is recommended to use the compiled library or the module library for improved build times. There are three primary ways to use {fmt} with CMake: & 10; & 10; FetchContent : Starting from CMake 3.11, you can use FetchContent to automatically& 10; download {fmt} as a dependency at configure time: & 10; include(FetchContent)& 10;& 10;FetchContent_Declare(& 10; fmt& 10; GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt& 10; GIT_TAG e69e5f977d458f2650bb346dadf2ad30c5320281) 10.2.1& 10;FetchContent_MakeAvailable(fmt)& 10;& 10;target_link_libraries(<your-target> fmt::fmt) & 10; & 10; & 10; Installed : You can find and use an installed version of& 10; {fmt} in your CMakeLists.txt file as follows: & 10; find_package(fmt)& 10;target_link_libraries(<your-target> fmt::fmt) & 10; & 10; & 10; Embedded : You can add the {fmt} source tree to your project and include it& 10; in your CMakeLists.txt file: & 10; add_subdirectory(fmt)& 10;target_link_libraries(<your-target> fmt::fmt) & 10; & 10; Alternative Targets In order to use the header-only target or the module target, simply substitute the fmt::fmt in the above steps with fmt::fmt-header-only or fmt::fmt-module accordingly. Installation Debian/Ubuntu To install {fmt} on Debian, Ubuntu, or any other Debian-based Linux distribution, use the following command: apt install libfmt-dev Homebrew Install {fmt} on macOS using Homebrew: brew install fmt Conda Install {fmt} on Linux, macOS, and Windows with Conda, using its conda-forge package: conda install -c conda-forge fmt vcpkg Download and install {fmt} using the vcpkg package manager: git clone https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg.git& 10;cd vcpkg& 10;./bootstrap-vcpkg.sh& 10;./vcpkg integrate install& 10;./vcpkg install fmt Conan You can download and install {fmt} using the Conan package manager: conan install -r conancenter --requires="fmt/[ ]" --build=missing Building from Source CMake works by generating native makefiles or project files that can be used in the compiler environment of your choice. The typical workflow starts with: mkdir build Create a directory to hold the build output.& 10;cd build& 10;cmake .. Generate native build scripts. run in the fmt repository. If you are on a Unix-like system, you should now see a Makefile in the current directory. Now you can build the library by running make . Once the library has been built you can invoke make test to run the tests. You can control generation of the make test target with the FMT_TEST CMake option. This can be useful if you include fmt as a subdirectory in your project but don't want to add fmt's tests to your test target. To build a shared library set the BUILD_SHARED_LIBS CMake variable to TRUE : cmake -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=TRUE .. To build a static library with position-independent code (e.g. for linking it into another shared library such as a Python extension), set the CMAKE_POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE CMake variable to TRUE : cmake -DCMAKE_POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE=TRUE .. After building the library you can install it on a Unix-like system by running sudo make install . Building the Docs To build the documentation you need the following software installed on your system: - Python - Doxygen - MkDocs with mkdocs-material , mkdocstrings , pymdown-extensions and mike First generate makefiles or project files using CMake as described in the previous section. Then compile the doc target/project, for example: make doc This will generate the HTML documentation in doc/html . Build Systems build2 You can use build2, a dependency manager and a build system, to use {fmt}. Currently this package is available in these package repositories: - for released and published versions. - for unreleased or custom versions. Usage: - build2 package name: fmt - Library target name: lib{fmt} To make your build2 project depend on fmt : & 10; & 10; Add one of the repositories to your configurations, or in your& 10; repositories.manifest , if not already there: & 10; :& 10;role: prerequisite& 10;location: https://pkg.cppget.org/1/stable & 10; & 10; & 10; Add this package as a dependency to your manifest file (example& 10; for version 10): & 10; depends: fmt 10.0.0 & 10; & 10; & 10; Import the target and use it as a prerequisite to your own target& 10; using fmt in the appropriate buildfile : & 10; import fmt = fmt%lib{fmt}& 10;lib{mylib} : cxx{ } ... $fmt & 10; & 10; Then build your project as usual with b or bdep update . Meson Meson WrapDB includes an fmt package. Usage: & 10; Install the fmt subproject from the WrapDB by running: meson wrap install fmt & 10; & 10; from the root of your project. & 10; & 10; In your project's meson.build file, add an entry for the new subproject: & 10; fmt = subproject('fmt')& 10;fmt_dep = fmt.get_variable('fmt_dep') & 10; & 10; & 10; Include the new dependency object to link with fmt: & 10; my_build_target = executable(& 10; 'name', 'src/main.cc', dependencies: [fmt_dep]) & 10; & 10; Options: If desired, {fmt} can be built as a static library, or as a header-only library. For a static build, use the following subproject definition: fmt = subproject('fmt', default_options: 'default_library=static')& 10;fmt_dep = fmt.get_variable('fmt_dep') For the header-only version, use: fmt = subproject('fmt', default_options: ['header-only=true'])& 10;fmt_dep = fmt.get_variable('fmt_header_only_dep') Android NDK {fmt} provides Android.mk file that can be used to build the library with Android NDK. Other To use the {fmt} library with any other build system, add include/fmt/base.h , include/fmt/format.h , include/fmt/format-inl.h , src/format.cc and optionally other headers from a release archive or the git repository to your project, add include to include directories and make sure src/format.cc is compiled and linked with your code.

entries.title: API Reference
entries.text: API Reference The {fmt} library API consists of the following components: - fmt/base.h : the base API providing main formatting functions for char /UTF-8 with C++20 compile-time checks and minimal dependencies - fmt/format.h : fmt::format and other formatting functions as well as locale support - fmt/ranges.h : formatting of ranges and tuples - fmt/chrono.h : date and time formatting - fmt/std.h : formatters for standard library types - fmt/compile.h : format string compilation - fmt/color.h : terminal colors and text styles - fmt/os.h : system APIs - fmt/ostream.h : std::ostream support - fmt/args.h : dynamic argument lists - fmt/printf.h : safe printf - fmt/xchar.h : optional wchar_t support All functions and types provided by the library reside in namespace fmt and macros have prefix FMT . C++ Module API With the C++ module API, the headers listed above don't need to be included. You can use the import fmt; statement instead. All other functionality, listed below, remains the same. Base API fmt/base.h defines the base API which provides main formatting functions for char /UTF-8 with C++20 compile-time checks. It has minimal include dependencies for better compile times. This header is only beneficial when using {fmt} as a library (the default) and not in the header-only mode. It also provides formatter specializations for the following types: - int , long long - unsigned , unsigned long long - float , double , long double - bool - char - const char , fmt::string_view - const void The following functions use format string syntax similar to that of str.format in Python. They take fmt and args as arguments. fmt is a format string that contains literal text and replacement fields surrounded by braces {} . The fields are replaced with formatted arguments in the resulting string. fmt::format_string is a format string which can be implicitly constructed from a string literal or a constexpr string and is checked at compile time in C++20. To pass a runtime format string wrap it in fmt::runtime . args is an argument list representing objects to be formatted. I/O errors are reported as std::system_error exceptions unless specified otherwise. & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; void print(format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt and writes the output to stdout . & 10; Example : fmt::print("The answer is {}.", 42);& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; void print(FILE f, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt and writes the output to the file f . & 10; Example : fmt::print(stderr, "Don't {}!", "panic");& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; void println(format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt and writes the output to stdout followed by a newline. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; void println(FILE f, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt and writes the output to the file f followed by a newline. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename OutputIt, typename... T>& 10; remove_cvref_t<OutputIt> format_to(OutputIt&& out, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt , writes the result to the output iterator out and returns the iterator past the end of the output range. format_to does not append a terminating null character. & 10; Example : auto out = std::vector<char>();& 10;fmt::format_to(std::back_inserter(out), "{}", 42);& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename OutputIt, typename... T>& 10; format_to_n_result<OutputIt> format_to_n(OutputIt out, size_t n, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt , writes up to n characters of the result to the output iterator out and returns the total (not truncated) output size and the iterator past the end of the output range. format_to_n does not append a terminating null character. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename OutputIt>& 10; struct format_to_n_result; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; OutputIt out; & 10; & 10; Iterator past the end of the output range. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; size_t size; & 10; & 10; Total (not truncated) output size. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; size_t formatted_size(format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Returns the number of chars in the output of format(fmt, args...) . & 10; & 10; Formatting User-Defined Types The {fmt} library provides formatters for many standard C++ types. See fmt/ranges.h for ranges and tuples including standard containers such as std::vector , fmt/chrono.h for date and time formatting and fmt/std.h for other standard library types. There are two ways to make a user-defined type formattable: providing a format_as function or specializing the formatter struct template. Formatting of non-void pointer types is intentionally disallowed and they cannot be made formattable via either extension API. Use format_as if you want to make your type formattable as some other type with the same format specifiers. The format_as function should take an object of your type and return an object of a formattable type. It should be defined in the same namespace as your type. Example (run): include <fmt/format.h>& 10;& 10;namespace kevin_namespacy {& 10;& 10;enum class film {& 10; house_of_cards, american_beauty, se7en = 7& 10;};& 10;& 10;auto format_as(film f) { return fmt::underlying(f); }& 10;& 10;}& 10;& 10;int main() {& 10; fmt::print("{}\n", kevin_namespacy::film::se7en); // Output: 7& 10;} Using a specialization is more complex, but gives you full control over parsing and formatting. To use this method, specialize the formatter struct template for your type and implement parse and format methods. The recommended way of defining a formatter is by reusing an existing one via inheritance or composition. This way you can support standard format specifiers without implementing them yourself. For example: // color.h:& 10; include <fmt/base.h>& 10;& 10;enum class color {red, green, blue};& 10;& 10;template <> struct fmt::formatter<color>: formatter<string_view> {& 10; // parse is inherited from formatter<string_view>.& 10;& 10; auto format(color c, format_context& ctx) const& 10; -> format_context::iterator;& 10;};& 10; // color.cc:& 10; include "color.h"& 10; include <fmt/format.h>& 10;& 10;auto fmt::formatter<color>::format(color c, format_context& ctx) const& 10; -> format_context::iterator {& 10; string_view name = "unknown";& 10; switch (c) {& 10; case color::red: name = "red"; break;& 10; case color::green: name = "green"; break;& 10; case color::blue: name = "blue"; break;& 10; }& 10; return formatter<string_view>::format(name, ctx);& 10;}& 10; Note that formatter ::format is defined in fmt/format.h so it has to be included in the source file. Since parse is inherited from formatter it will recognize all string format specifications, for example fmt::format("{:>10}", color::blue)& 10; will return " blue" . In general the formatter has the following form: template <> struct fmt::formatter<T> {& 10; // Parses format specifiers and stores them in the formatter.& 10; //& 10; // ctx.begin(), ctx.end()) is a, possibly empty, character range that& 10; // contains a part of the format string starting from the format& 10; // specifications to be parsed, e.g. in& 10; //& 10; // fmt::format("{:f} continued", ...);& 10; //& 10; // the range will contain "f} continued". The formatter should parse& 10; // specifiers until '}' or the end of the range. In this example the& 10; // formatter should parse the 'f' specifier and return an iterator& 10; // pointing to '}'.& 10; constexpr auto parse(format_parse_context& ctx)& 10; -> format_parse_context::iterator;& 10;& 10; // Formats value using the parsed format specification stored in this& 10; // formatter and writes the output to ctx.out().& 10; auto format(const T& value, format_context& ctx) const& 10; -> format_context::iterator;& 10;}; It is recommended to at least support fill, align and width that apply to the whole object and have the same semantics as in standard formatters. You can also write a formatter for a hierarchy of classes: // demo.h:& 10; include <type_traits>& 10; include <fmt/format.h>& 10;& 10;struct A {& 10; virtual A() {}& 10; virtual std::string name() const { return "A"; }& 10;};& 10;& 10;struct B : A {& 10; virtual std::string name() const { return "B"; }& 10;};& 10;& 10;template <typename T>& 10;struct fmt::formatter<T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_base_of_v<A, T>, char>> :& 10; fmt::formatter<std::string> {& 10; auto format(const A& a, format_context& ctx) const {& 10; return formatter<std::string>::format(a.name(), ctx);& 10; }& 10;};& 10; // demo.cc:& 10; include "demo.h"& 10; include <fmt/format.h>& 10;& 10;int main() {& 10; B b;& 10; A& a = b;& 10; fmt::print("{}", a); // Output: B& 10;}& 10; Providing both a formatter specialization and a format_as overload is disallowed. & 10; & 10; template <typename Char>& 10; using basic_format_parse_context = parse_context<Char>; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; class context; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; constexpr context(iterator out, format_args args, locale_ref loc); & 10; & 10; Constructs a context object. References to the arguments are stored in the object so make sure they have appropriate lifetimes. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; using format_context = context; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Compile-Time Checks Compile-time format string checks are enabled by default on compilers that support C++20 consteval . On older compilers you can use the [FMT_STRING macro defined in fmt/format.h instead. Unused arguments are allowed as in Python's str.format and ordinary functions. See Type Erasure for an example of how to enable compile-time checks in your own functions with fmt::format_string while avoiding template bloat. & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; struct fstring; & 10; & 10; & 10; A compile-time format string. Use format_string in the public API to prevent type deduction. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; using format_string = typename fstring<T...>::t; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; runtime_format_string<> runtime(string_view s); & 10; & 10; & 10; Creates a runtime format string. & 10; Example : // Check format string at runtime instead of compile-time.& 10;fmt::print(fmt::runtime("{:d}"), "I am not a number");& 10; & 10; & 10; Type Erasure You can create your own formatting function with compile-time checks and small binary footprint, for example (run): include <fmt/format.h>& 10;& 10;void vlog(const char file, int line,& 10; fmt::string_view fmt, fmt::format_args args) {& 10; fmt::print("{}: {}: {}", file, line, fmt::vformat(fmt, args));& 10;}& 10;& 10;template <typename... T>& 10;void log(const char file, int line,& 10; fmt::format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args) {& 10; vlog(file, line, fmt, fmt::make_format_args(args...));& 10;}& 10;& 10; define MY_LOG(fmt, ...) log( FILE , LINE , fmt, VA_ARGS )& 10;& 10;MY_LOG("invalid squishiness: {}", 42);& 10; Note that vlog is not parameterized on argument types which improves compile times and reduces binary code size compared to a fully parameterized version. & 10; & 10; template <typename Context, typename... T, int NUM_ARGS, int NUM_NAMED_ARGS, ullong DESC>& 10; detail::format_arg_store<Context, NUM_ARGS, NUM_NAMED_ARGS, DESC> make_format_args(T&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Constructs an object that stores references to arguments and can be implicitly converted to format_args . Context can be omitted in which case it defaults to context . See arg for lifetime considerations. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename Context>& 10; class basic_format_args; & 10; & 10; & 10; A view of a collection of formatting arguments. To avoid lifetime issues it should only be used as a parameter type in type-erased functions such as vformat : void vlog(fmt::string_view fmt, fmt::format_args args); // OK& 10;fmt::format_args args = fmt::make_format_args(); // Dangling reference& 10; & 10; & 10; constexpr basic_format_args(const store<NUM_ARGS, NUM_NAMED_ARGS, DESC>& s); & 10; & 10; Constructs a basic_format_args object from format_arg_store . & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; constexpr basic_format_args(const format_arg args, int count, bool has_named); & 10; & 10; Constructs a basic_format_args object from a dynamic list of arguments. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; format_arg get(int id); & 10; & 10; Returns the argument with the specified id. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; using format_args = basic_format_args<context>; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename Context>& 10; class basic_format_arg; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; decltype(vis(0)) visit(Visitor&& vis); & 10; & 10; Visits an argument dispatching to the appropriate visit method based on the argument type. For example, if the argument type is double then vis(value) will be called with the value of type double . & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Named Arguments & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; named_arg<T> arg(const char name, const T& arg); & 10; & 10; & 10; Returns a named argument to be used in a formatting function. It should only be used in a call to a formatting function. & 10; Example : fmt::print("The answer is {answer}.", fmt::arg("answer", 42));& 10; & 10; Named arguments passed with fmt::arg are not supported in compile-time checks, but "answer" a=42 are compile-time checked in sufficiently new compilers. See operator"" a() . & 10; & 10; Compatibility & 10; & 10; template <typename Char>& 10; class basic_string_view; & 10; & 10; & 10; An implementation of std::basic_string_view for pre-C++17 providing a subset of the API. fmt::basic_string_view is used in the public API even if std::basic_string_view is available to prevent issues when a library is compiled with a different -std option than the client code (which is not recommended). & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; using string_view = basic_string_view<char>; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Format API fmt/format.h defines the full format API providing additional formatting functions and locale support. & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; std::string format(format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt and returns the result as a string. & 10; Example : include <fmt/format.h>& 10;std::string message = fmt::format("The answer is {}.", 42);& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; std::string vformat(string_view fmt, format_args args); & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <detail::fixed_string S>& 10; auto operator"" a(); & 10; & 10; & 10; User-defined literal equivalent of fmt::arg , but with compile-time checks. & 10; Example : using namespace fmt::literals;& 10;fmt::print("The answer is {answer}.", "answer" a=42);& 10; & 10; & 10; Utilities & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; const void ptr(T p); & 10; & 10; & 10; Converts p to const void for pointer formatting. & 10; Example : auto s = fmt::format("{}", fmt::ptr(p));& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename Enum>& 10; underlying_t<Enum> underlying(Enum e); & 10; & 10; & 10; Converts e to the underlying type. & 10; Example : enum class color { red, green, blue };& 10;auto s = fmt::format("{}", fmt::underlying(color::red)); // s == "0"& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; std::string to_string(const T& value); & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; group_digits_view<T> group_digits(T value); & 10; & 10; & 10; Returns a view that formats an integer value using ',' as a locale-independent thousands separator. & 10; Example : fmt::print("{}", fmt::group_digits(12345));& 10;// Output: "12,345"& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; class detail::buffer; & 10; & 10; & 10; A contiguous memory buffer with an optional growing ability. It is an internal class and shouldn't be used directly, only via memory_buffer . & 10; & 10; size_t size(); & 10; & 10; Returns the size of this buffer. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; size_t capacity(); & 10; & 10; Returns the capacity of this buffer. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; T data(); & 10; & 10; Returns a pointer to the buffer data (not null-terminated). & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; void clear(); & 10; & 10; Clears this buffer. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; void append(const U begin, const U end); & 10; & 10; Appends data to the end of the buffer. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename T, size_t SIZE, typename Allocator>& 10; class basic_memory_buffer; & 10; & 10; & 10; A dynamically growing memory buffer for trivially copyable/constructible types with the first SIZE elements stored in the object itself. Most commonly used via the memory_buffer alias for char . & 10; Example : auto out = fmt::memory_buffer();& 10;fmt::format_to(std::back_inserter(out), "The answer is {}.", 42);& 10; & 10; This will append "The answer is 42." to out . The buffer content can be converted to std::string with to_string(out) . & 10; & 10; basic_memory_buffer(basic_memory_buffer&& other); & 10; & 10; Constructs a basic_memory_buffer object moving the content of the other object to it. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; basic_memory_buffer & operator=(basic_memory_buffer&& other); & 10; & 10; Moves the content of the other basic_memory_buffer object to this one. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; void resize(size_t count); & 10; & 10; Resizes the buffer to contain count elements. If T is a POD type new elements may not be initialized. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; void reserve(size_t new_capacity); & 10; & 10; Increases the buffer capacity to new_capacity . & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; System Errors {fmt} does not use errno to communicate errors to the user, but it may call system functions which set errno . Users should not make any assumptions about the value of errno being preserved by library functions. & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; std::system_error system_error(int error_code, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Constructs std::system_error with a message formatted with fmt::format(fmt, args...) . error_code is a system error code as given by errno . & 10; Example : // This throws std::system_error with the description& 10;// cannot open file 'madeup': No such file or directory& 10;// or similar (system message may vary).& 10;const char filename = "madeup";& 10;FILE file = fopen(filename, "r");& 10;if (!file)& 10; throw fmt::system_error(errno, "cannot open file '{}'", filename);& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; void format_system_error(detail::buffer<char>& out, int error_code, const char message); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats an error message for an error returned by an operating system or a language runtime, for example a file opening error, and writes it to out . The format is the same as the one used by std::system_error(ec, message) where ec is std::error_code(error_code, std::generic_category()) . It is implementation-defined but normally looks like: <message>: <system-message>& 10; & 10; where <message> is the passed message and <system-message> is the system message corresponding to the error code. error_code is a system error code as given by errno . & 10; & 10; Custom Allocators The {fmt} library supports custom dynamic memory allocators. A custom allocator class can be specified as a template argument to fmt::basic_memory_buffer : using custom_memory_buffer = & 10; fmt::basic_memory_buffer<char, fmt::inline_buffer_size, custom_allocator>; It is also possible to write a formatting function that uses a custom allocator: using custom_string =& 10; std::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, custom_allocator>;& 10;& 10;auto vformat(custom_allocator alloc, fmt::string_view fmt,& 10; fmt::format_args args) -> custom_string {& 10; auto buf = custom_memory_buffer(alloc);& 10; fmt::vformat_to(std::back_inserter(buf), fmt, args);& 10; return custom_string(buf.data(), buf.size(), alloc);& 10;}& 10;& 10;template <typename ...Args>& 10;auto format(custom_allocator alloc, fmt::string_view fmt,& 10; const Args& ... args) -> custom_string {& 10; return vformat(alloc, fmt, fmt::make_format_args(args...));& 10;} The allocator will be used for the output container only. Formatting functions normally don't do any allocations for built-in and string types except for non-default floating-point formatting that occasionally falls back on sprintf . Locale All formatting is locale-independent by default. Use the 'L' format specifier to insert the appropriate number separator characters from the locale: include <fmt/format.h>& 10; include <locale>& 10;& 10;std::locale::global(std::locale("en_US.UTF-8"));& 10;auto s = fmt::format("{:L}", 1000000); // s == "1,000,000" fmt/format.h provides the following overloads of formatting functions that take std::locale as a parameter. The locale type is a template parameter to avoid the expensive include. & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; std::string format(locale_ref loc, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename OutputIt, typename... T>& 10; OutputIt format_to(OutputIt out, locale_ref loc, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; size_t formatted_size(locale_ref loc, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Legacy Compile-Time Checks FMT_STRING enables compile-time checks on older compilers. It requires C++14 or later and is a no-op in C++11. & 10; & 10; FMT_STRING(s) & 10; & 10; & 10; Constructs a legacy compile-time format string from a string literal s . & 10; Example : // A compile-time error because 'd' is an invalid specifier for strings.& 10;std::string s = fmt::format(FMT_STRING("{:d}"), "foo");& 10; & 10; & 10; To force the use of legacy compile-time checks, define the preprocessor variable FMT_ENFORCE_COMPILE_STRING . When set, functions accepting FMT_STRING will fail to compile with regular strings. Range and Tuple Formatting fmt/ranges.h provides formatting support for ranges and tuples: include <fmt/ranges.h>& 10;& 10;fmt::print("{}", std::tuple<char, int>{'a', 42});& 10;// Output: ('a', 42) Using fmt::join , you can separate tuple elements with a custom separator: include <fmt/ranges.h>& 10;& 10;auto t = std::tuple<int, char>{1, 'a'};& 10;fmt::print("{}", fmt::join(t, ", "));& 10;// Output: 1, a & 10; & 10; template <typename Range>& 10; join_view<decltype(detail::range_begin(r)), decltype(detail::range_end(r))> join(Range&& r, string_view sep); & 10; & 10; & 10; Returns a view that formats range with elements separated by sep . & 10; Example : auto v = std::vector<int>{1, 2, 3};& 10;fmt::print("{}", fmt::join(v, ", "));& 10;// Output: 1, 2, 3& 10; & 10; fmt::join applies passed format specifiers to the range elements: fmt::print("{:02}", fmt::join(v, ", "));& 10;// Output: 01, 02, 03& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename It, typename Sentinel>& 10; join_view<It, Sentinel> join(It begin, Sentinel end, string_view sep); & 10; & 10; & 10; Returns a view that formats the iterator range begin, end) with elements separated by sep . & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; join_view<const T , const T > join(std::initializer_list<T> list, string_view sep); & 10; & 10; & 10; Returns an object that formats std::initializer_list with elements separated by sep . & 10; Example : fmt::print("{}", fmt::join({1, 2, 3}, ", "));& 10;// Output: "1, 2, 3"& 10; & 10; & 10; Date and Time Formatting fmt/chrono.h provides formatters for - [ std::chrono::duration - std::chrono::time_point - std::tm The format syntax is described in Chrono Format Specifications. Example : include <fmt/chrono.h>& 10;& 10;int main() {& 10; auto now = std::chrono::system_clock::now();& 10;& 10; fmt::print("The date is {:%Y-%m-%d}.\n", now);& 10; // Output: The date is 2020-11-07.& 10; // (with 2020-11-07 replaced by the current date)& 10;& 10; using namespace std::literals::chrono_literals;& 10;& 10; fmt::print("Default format: {} {}\n", 42s, 100ms);& 10; // Output: Default format: 42s 100ms& 10;& 10; fmt::print("strftime-like format: {:%H:%M:%S}\n", 3h + 15min + 30s);& 10; // Output: strftime-like format: 03:15:30& 10;} & 10; & 10; std::tm gmtime(std::time_t time); & 10; & 10; & 10; Converts given time since epoch as std::time_t value into calendar time, expressed in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Unlike std::gmtime , this function is thread-safe on most platforms. & 10; & 10; Standard Library Types Formatting fmt/std.h provides formatters for: - std::atomic - std::atomic_flag - std::bitset - std::error_code - std::exception - std::filesystem::path - std::monostate - std::optional - std::source_location - std::thread::id - std::variant & 10; & 10; template <typename T, typename Deleter>& 10; const void ptr(const std::unique_ptr<T, Deleter>& p); & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; const void ptr(const std::shared_ptr<T>& p); & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Variants A std::variant can be formatted only if every alternative is formattable, and requires the cpp_lib_variant library feature. Example : include <fmt/std.h>& 10;& 10;fmt::print("{}", std::variant<char, float>('x'));& 10;// Output: variant('x')& 10;& 10;fmt::print("{}", std::variant<std::monostate, char>());& 10;// Output: variant(monostate) Bit-Fields and Packed Structs To format a bit-field or a field of a struct with attribute ((packed)) applied to it, you need to convert it to the underlying or compatible type via a cast or a unary + (godbolt): struct smol {& 10; int bit : 1;& 10;};& 10;& 10;auto s = smol();& 10;fmt::print("{}", +s.bit);& 10; This is a known limitation of "perfect" forwarding in C++. Compile-Time Support fmt/compile.h provides format string compilation and compile-time ( constexpr ) formatting enabled via the FMT_COMPILE macro or the cf user-defined literal defined in namespace fmt::literals . Format strings marked with FMT_COMPILE or cf are parsed, checked and converted into efficient formatting code at compile-time. This supports arguments of built-in and string types as well as user-defined types with format methods taking the format context type as a template parameter in their formatter specializations. For example (run): struct point {& 10; double x;& 10; double y;& 10;};& 10;& 10;template <> struct fmt::formatter<point> {& 10; constexpr auto parse(format_parse_context& ctx) { return ctx.begin(); }& 10;& 10; template <typename FormatContext>& 10; auto format(const point& p, FormatContext& ctx) const {& 10; return format_to(ctx.out(), "({}, {})" cf, p.x, p.y);& 10; }& 10;};& 10;& 10;using namespace fmt::literals;& 10;std::string s = fmt::format("{}" cf, point(4, 2)); Format string compilation can generate more binary code compared to the default API and is only recommended in places where formatting is a performance bottleneck. The same APIs support formatting at compile time e.g. in constexpr and consteval functions. Additionally there is an experimental FMT_STATIC_FORMAT that allows formatting into a string of the exact required size at compile time. Compile-time formatting works with built-in and user-defined formatters that have constexpr format methods. Example: template <> struct fmt::formatter<point> {& 10; constexpr auto parse(format_parse_context& ctx) { return ctx.begin(); }& 10;& 10; template <typename FormatContext>& 10; constexpr auto format(const point& p, FormatContext& ctx) const {& 10; return format_to(ctx.out(), "({}, {})" cf, p.x, p.y);& 10; }& 10;};& 10;& 10;constexpr auto s = FMT_STATIC_FORMAT("{}", point(4, 2));& 10;const char cstr = s.c_str(); // Points the static string "(4, 2)". & 10; & 10; template <detail::fixed_string Str>& 10; auto operator"" cf(); & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; FMT_COMPILE(s) & 10; & 10; & 10; Converts a string literal s into a format string that will be parsed at compile time and converted into efficient formatting code. Requires C++17 constexpr if compiler support. & 10; Example : // Converts 42 into std::string using the most efficient method and no& 10;// runtime format string processing.& 10;std::string s = fmt::format(FMT_COMPILE("{}"), 42);& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; FMT_STATIC_FORMAT(fmt_str, ...) & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats arguments according to the format string fmt_str and produces a string of the exact required size at compile time. Both the format string and the arguments must be compile-time expressions. & 10; The resulting string can be accessed as a C string via c_str() or as a fmt::string_view via str() . & 10; Example : // Produces the static string "42" at compile time.& 10;static constexpr auto result = FMT_STATIC_FORMAT("{}", 42);& 10;const char s = result.c_str();& 10; & 10; & 10; Terminal Colors and Text Styles fmt/color.h provides support for terminal color and text style output. & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; void print(text_style ts, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats a string and prints it to stdout using ANSI escape sequences to specify text formatting. & 10; Example : fmt::print(fmt::emphasis::bold fg(fmt::color::red),& 10; "Elapsed time: {0:.2f} seconds", 1.23);& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; text_style fg(detail::color_type foreground); & 10; & 10; & 10; Creates a text style from the foreground (text) color. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; text_style bg(detail::color_type background); & 10; & 10; & 10; Creates a text style from the background color. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; detail::styled_arg<remove_cvref_t<T>> styled(const T& value, text_style ts); & 10; & 10; & 10; Returns an argument that will be formatted using ANSI escape sequences, to be used in a formatting function. & 10; Example : fmt::print("Elapsed time: {0:.2f} seconds",& 10; fmt::styled(1.23, fmt::fg(fmt::color::green) & 10; fmt::bg(fmt::color::blue)));& 10; & 10; & 10; System APIs & 10; & 10; class ostream; & 10; & 10; & 10; A fast buffered output stream for writing from a single thread. Writing from multiple threads without external synchronization may result in a data race. & 10; & 10; void print(format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt and writes the output to the file. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; ostream output_file(cstring_view path, T... params); & 10; & 10; & 10; Opens a file for writing. Supported parameters passed in params : & 10; & 10; <integer> : Flags passed to open ( file::WRONLY file::CREATE file::TRUNC by default) & 10; buffer_size=<integer> : Output buffer size & 10; & 10; & 10; Example : auto out = fmt::output_file("guide.txt");& 10;out.print("Don't {}", "Panic");& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; std::system_error windows_error(int error_code, string_view message, const T&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Constructs a std::system_error object with the description of the form <message>: <system-message>& 10; & 10; where <message> is the formatted message and <system-message> is the system message corresponding to the error code. error_code is a Windows error code as given by GetLastError . If error_code is not a valid error code such as -1, the system message will look like "error -1". & 10; Example : // This throws a system_error with the description& 10;// cannot open file 'foo': The system cannot find the file specified.& 10;// or similar (system message may vary) if the file doesn't exist.& 10;const char filename = "foo";& 10;LPOFSTRUCT of = LPOFSTRUCT();& 10;HFILE file = OpenFile(filename, &of, OF_READ);& 10;if (file == HFILE_ERROR) {& 10; throw fmt::windows_error(GetLastError(),& 10; "cannot open file '{}'", filename);& 10;}& 10; & 10; & 10; std::ostream Support fmt/ostream.h provides std::ostream support including formatting of user-defined types that have an overloaded insertion operator ( operator include <fmt/ostream.h>& 10;& 10;struct date {& 10; int year, month, day;& 10;& 10; friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const date& d) {& 10; return os << d.year << '-' << d.month << '-' << d.day;& 10; }& 10;};& 10;& 10;template <> struct fmt::formatter<date> : ostream_formatter {};& 10;& 10;std::string s = fmt::format("The date is {}", date{2012, 12, 9});& 10;// s == "The date is 2012-12-9" & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; detail::streamed_view<T> streamed(const T& value); & 10; & 10; & 10; Returns a view that formats value via an ostream operator<< . & 10; Example : fmt::print("Current thread id: {}\n",& 10; fmt::streamed(std::this_thread::get_id()));& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; void print(std::ostream& os, format_string<T...> fmt, T&&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Prints formatted data to the stream os . & 10; Example : fmt::print(cerr, "Don't {}!", "panic");& 10; & 10; & 10; Dynamic Argument Lists The header fmt/args.h provides dynamic_format_arg_store , a builder-like API that can be used to construct format argument lists dynamically. & 10; & 10; template <typename Context>& 10; class dynamic_format_arg_store; & 10; & 10; & 10; A dynamic list of formatting arguments with storage. & 10; It can be implicitly converted into fmt::basic_format_args for passing into type-erased formatting functions such as fmt::vformat . & 10; & 10; void push_back(const T& arg); & 10; & 10; Adds an argument into the dynamic store for later passing to a formatting function. & 10; Note that custom types and string types (but not string views) are copied into the store dynamically allocating memory if necessary. & 10; Example : fmt::dynamic_format_arg_store<fmt::format_context> store;& 10;store.push_back(42);& 10;store.push_back("abc");& 10;store.push_back(1.5f);& 10;std::string result = fmt::vformat("{} and {} and {}", store);& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; void push_back(std::reference_wrapper<T> arg); & 10; & 10; Adds a reference to the argument into the dynamic store for later passing to a formatting function. & 10; Example : fmt::dynamic_format_arg_store<fmt::format_context> store;& 10;char band[] = "Rolling Stones";& 10;store.push_back(std::cref(band));& 10;band[9] = 'c'; // Changing str affects the output.& 10;std::string result = fmt::vformat("{}", store);& 10;// result == "Rolling Scones"& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; void push_back(const named_arg<T, char_type>& arg); & 10; & 10; Adds named argument into the dynamic store for later passing to a formatting function. std::reference_wrapper is supported to avoid copying of the argument. The name is always copied into the store. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; void clear(); & 10; & 10; Erase all elements from the store. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; void reserve(size_t new_cap, size_t new_cap_named); & 10; & 10; Reserves space to store at least new_cap arguments including new_cap_named named arguments. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; size_t size(); & 10; & 10; Returns the number of elements in the store. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Safe printf The header fmt/printf.h provides printf -like formatting functionality. The following functions use printf format string syntax with the POSIX extension for positional arguments. Unlike their standard counterparts, the fmt functions are type-safe and throw an exception if an argument type doesn't match its format specification. & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; int printf(string_view fmt, const T&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt and writes the output to stdout . & 10; Example : & 10; fmt::printf("Elapsed time: %.2f seconds", 1.23); & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; int fprintf(std::FILE f, string_view fmt, const T&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt and writes the output to f . & 10; Example : fmt::fprintf(stderr, "Don't %s!", "panic");& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename... T>& 10; std::string sprintf(string_view fmt, const T&... args); & 10; & 10; & 10; Formats args according to specifications in fmt and returns the result as string. & 10; Example : std::string message = fmt::sprintf("The answer is %d", 42);& 10; & 10; & 10; Wide Strings The optional header fmt/xchar.h provides support for wchar_t and exotic character types. & 10; & 10; using wstring_view = basic_string_view<wchar_t>; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; using wformat_context = buffered_context<wchar_t>; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; template <typename T>& 10; std::wstring to_wstring(const T& value); & 10; & 10; & 10; Converts value to std::wstring using the default format for type T . & 10; & 10; Compatibility with C++20 std::format {fmt} implements nearly all of the C++20 formatting library with the following differences: - Names are defined in the fmt namespace instead of std to avoid collisions with standard library implementations. - Width calculation doesn't use grapheme clusterization. The latter has been implemented in a separate branch but hasn't been integrated yet. - The default floating-point representation in {fmt} uses the smallest precision that provides round-trip guarantees similarly to other languages like Java and Python. std::format is currently specified in terms of std::to_chars which tries to generate the smallest number of characters (ignoring redundant digits and sign in exponent) and may produce more decimal digits than necessary. Configuration Options {fmt} provides configuration via CMake options and preprocessor macros to enable or disable features and to optimize for binary size. For example, you can disable OS-specific APIs defined in fmt/os.h with -DFMT_OS=OFF when configuring CMake. CMake Options - FMT_OS : When set to OFF , disables OS-specific APIs ( fmt/os.h ). - FMT_UNICODE : When set to OFF , disables Unicode support on Windows/MSVC. Unicode support is always enabled on other platforms. Macros - FMT_HEADER_ONLY : Enables the header-only mode when defined. It is an alternative to using the fmt::fmt-header-only CMake target. Default: not defined. - FMT_USE_EXCEPTIONS : Disables the use of exceptions when set to 0 . Default: 1 ( 0 if compiled with -fno-exceptions ). - FMT_USE_LOCALE : When set to 0 , disables locale support. Default: 1 ( 0 when FMT_OPTIMIZE_SIZE 1 ). - FMT_CUSTOM_ASSERT_FAIL : When set to 1 , allows users to provide a custom fmt::assert_fail function which is called on assertion failures and, if exceptions are disabled, on runtime errors. Default: 0 . - FMT_BUILTIN_TYPES : When set to 0 , disables built-in handling of arithmetic and string types other than int . This reduces library size at the cost of per-call overhead. Default: 1 . - FMT_OPTIMIZE_SIZE : Controls binary size optimizations: - 0 - off (default) - 1 - disables locale support and applies some optimizations - 2 - disables some Unicode features, named arguments and applies more aggressive optimizations Editorial note for fmt 12.2.0. The upstream list above says that FMT_OPTIMIZE_SIZE=1 disables locale support. However, the fixed-version header defines FMT_USE_LOCALE as (FMT_OPTIMIZE_SIZE <= 1) when it has not been explicitly defined. Therefore the default is enabled at level 1 and disabled at level 2. An explicit FMT_USE_LOCALE setting overrides that default. The original documentation wording is retained above. Binary Size Optimization To minimize the binary footprint of {fmt} as much as possible at the cost of some features, you can use the following configuration: - CMake options: - FMT_OS=OFF - Macros: - FMT_BUILTIN_TYPES=0 - FMT_OPTIMIZE_SIZE=2

entries.title: Format String Syntax
entries.text: Format String Syntax The formatting functions in this library — most notably fmt::format and fmt::print — accept format strings written in the syntax described here. A format string is plain text with embedded replacement fields delimited by the braces { and } . Characters outside of any replacement field are copied to the output unchanged. To emit a literal brace, double it: {{ yields a single { in the output, and }} yields a single } . A replacement field is described by the grammar below. replacement_field ::= "{" [arg_id] [":" ( format_spec chrono_format_spec )] "}"& 10;arg_id ::= integer identifier& 10;integer ::= digit+& 10;digit ::= "0"..."9"& 10;identifier ::= id_start id_continue & 10;id_start ::= "a"..."z" "A"..."Z" " "& 10;id_continue ::= id_start digit & 10; An arg_id selects which argument to format. It may be a non-negative integer (positional reference) or an identifier matching the name of an argument passed via fmt::arg (named reference). When arg_id is omitted, arguments are consumed in left-to-right order; this automatic indexing must be used uniformly throughout the format string — mixing automatic and explicit numeric ids is a compile-time error (or a format_error at runtime). A format_spec , introduced by : , describes how the value should be rendered. Its grammar is type-dependent; the form used by the standard built-in types is documented in the next section. For example: fmt::format("hello, {}", "world");& 10;// Result: "hello, world"& 10;& 10;fmt::format("{1}, {0}!", "world", "hello");& 10;// Result: "hello, world!"& 10;& 10;fmt::format("{greeting}, {name}!",& 10; fmt::arg("greeting", "hi"), fmt::arg("name", "fmt"));& 10;// Result: "hi, fmt!"& 10; A width or precision inside a format_spec may itself be written as a nested replacement field — {} or {arg_id} — in which case it takes its value from an integer argument at runtime. Nested fields accept only an arg_id ; they cannot themselves contain a format_spec . Format Specification The grammar below describes the format_spec shared by the built-in types — integers, floating-point values, characters, strings, booleans, and pointers — as well as by any user-defined type whose formatter reuses fmt's parser. format_spec ::= [[fill]align][sign][" "]["0"][width]["." precision]["L"][type]& 10;fill ::= <a character other than '{' or '}'>& 10;align ::= "<" ">" "^"& 10;sign ::= "+" "-" " "& 10;width ::= integer "{" [ arg_id ] "}"& 10;precision ::= integer "{" [ arg_id ] "}"& 10;type ::= "a" "A" "b" "B" "c" "d" "e" "E" "f" "F" & 10; "g" "G" "o" "p" "s" "x" "X" "?" & 10; Whether a particular option is meaningful depends on the value being formatted; options that do not apply to a value's type are diagnosed at compile time when possible and otherwise raise a format_error . Fill and alignment The align field selects where padding is placed when width makes the field wider than the value's natural rendering. & 10; & 10; & 10; Option & 10; Effect & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; < & 10; Left-align; pad on the right. Default for non-numeric types. & 10; & 10; & 10; > & 10; Right-align; pad on the left. Default for numeric types. & 10; & 10; & 10; ^ & 10; Center the value; if the padding cannot be split evenly, the extra padding character goes on the right. & 10; & 10; & 10; The fill character is any single Unicode code point other than { or } , encoded the same way as the format string. It supplies the padding character in place of the default space. A fill character is recognized only when it is immediately followed by an align character — otherwise it would be indistinguishable from an option in another position — so to use a custom fill you must also specify an alignment. Alignment has no observable effect when the value's natural rendering is already at least as wide as width ; the value is never truncated to fit. fmt::format("[{:<10}]", "42"); // Result: "[42 ]"& 10;fmt::format("[{:>10}]", "42"); // Result: "[ 42]"& 10;fmt::format("[{:^10}]", "42"); // Result: "[ 42 ]"& 10;fmt::format("[{: ^10}]", "42"); // Result: "[ 42 ]" - ' ' as fill& 10; Sign The sign field controls how the sign of a numeric value is emitted. It applies to signed integer and floating-point types only. & 10; & 10; & 10; Option & 10; Effect & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; + & 10; Always emit a sign ( + for nonnegative values, - for negative). & 10; & 10; & 10; - & 10; Emit - only for negative values. This is the default. & 10; & 10; & 10; space & 10; Emit a leading space for nonnegative values and - for negative ones; useful for aligning columns of signed numbers. & 10; & 10; & 10; The sign of -0.0 is preserved in floating-point output. fmt::format("{:+d} {:+d}", 7, -7); // Result: "+7 -7"& 10;fmt::format("{: d} {: d}", 7, -7); // Result: " 7 -7"& 10; Alternate form ( ) The flag selects an alternate form whose exact meaning depends on the presentation type: - For integers rendered in binary, octal, or hexadecimal, it prepends the appropriate base prefix ( 0b / 0B , 0 , or 0x / 0X ). The case of the prefix follows the case of the type specifier — 0x for x , 0X for X , and so on. - For floating-point values, it forces the decimal point to appear in the output even if no fractional digits would otherwise be emitted, and prevents the g / G presentation types from removing trailing zeros from the significand. The flag is not accepted by non-numeric types. Zero padding ( 0 ) A 0 placed immediately before width enables sign-aware zero padding for numeric types. Zeros are inserted between the sign (or base prefix, if any) and the most significant digit, so that a sign or 0x prefix stays adjacent to the digits rather than being separated by spaces. For example, {:+08d} applied to 120 produces +0000120 . Zero padding: - applies only to numeric types; - has no effect on inf or nan ; - is ignored when an explicit align is also present. Width width is a non-negative decimal integer giving the minimum number of characters that the field should occupy. If the formatted value is shorter than width , it is padded according to align and fill ; if it is longer, the value is written in full. width never causes the value to be truncated. To supply width at runtime, write the field as {} to consume the next argument, or as {arg_id} to reference an integer argument by position or by name. When formatting strings, "width" is measured in display columns using a Unicode-aware estimate (East Asian wide and fullwidth characters, plus common emoji ranges, count as two columns; everything else counts as one). This keeps fixed width values visually consistent in monospace renderings that combine Latin and CJK text. fmt::format("[{:6}]", 42);& 10;// Result: "[ 42]" - right-aligned by default& 10;fmt::format("[{:6}]", "hi");& 10;// Result: "[hi ]" - left-aligned by default& 10;fmt::format("[{:{}}]", 42, 6);& 10;// Result: "[ 42]" - width from an argument& 10; Precision precision is a non-negative decimal integer (introduced by . ) whose meaning depends on the value being formatted. As with width , it may be supplied as a nested replacement field for runtime evaluation. & 10; & 10; & 10; Type & 10; Meaning of .precision & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; e , E , f , F & 10; Digits emitted after the decimal point. & 10; & 10; & 10; g , G & 10; Total number of significant digits. & 10; & 10; & 10; a , A & 10; Digits after the decimal point in the hexadecimal significand. If omitted, just enough digits are emitted to round-trip the value exactly. & 10; & 10; & 10; Strings ( s , ? , or default) & 10; Upper bound on the number of code points copied from the value. & 10; & 10; & 10; A precision is not accepted for integer, character, boolean, or pointer types. When a precision limits the number of characters taken from a C string, the string must still be null-terminated. fmt::format("{:.2f}", 3.14159); // Result: "3.14"& 10;fmt::format("{:.3g}", 3.14159); // Result: "3.14"& 10;fmt::format("{:.4}", "hello, world"); // Result: "hell"& 10;fmt::format("{:.{}f}", 3.14159, 4);& 10;// Result: "3.1416" - precision from an argument& 10; Locale ( L ) The L flag selects locale-sensitive formatting for numeric types. The formatter inspects the C++ locale supplied to the formatting function (or the global locale, if none was passed) and inserts the locale's digit grouping characters and — for floating-point values — its decimal point. The flag has no effect on non-numeric types. auto loc = std::locale("en_US.UTF-8");& 10;fmt::format(loc, "{:L}", 1234567890); // Result: "1,234,567,890"& 10;fmt::format(loc, "{:.2Lf}", 1234567.89); // Result: "1,234,567.89"& 10; Presentation type The type field chooses the representation for the value. Specifiers are grouped below by the value categories they apply to. Integers, booleans, and characters: & 10; & 10; & 10; Type & 10; Effect & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; b & 10; Base 2. The flag adds a 0b prefix. & 10; & 10; & 10; B & 10; Base 2. The flag adds a 0B prefix. & 10; & 10; & 10; c & 10; Render the integer as the character with that code point. Not allowed for bool . & 10; & 10; & 10; d & 10; Base 10. The default for integer types. & 10; & 10; & 10; o & 10; Base 8. & 10; & 10; & 10; x & 10; Base 16, lower-case digits. The flag adds a 0x prefix. & 10; & 10; & 10; X & 10; Base 16, upper-case digits. The flag adds a 0X prefix. & 10; & 10; & 10; none & 10; Same as d for integers, c for characters, and the textual form ( true / false ) for bool . & 10; & 10; & 10; fmt::format("{:d} {: x} {: o} {: b}", 42, 42, 42, 42);& 10;// Result: "42 0x2a 052 0b101010"& 10;& 10;fmt::format("{: 06x}", 0xfe); // adds the prefix, 06 zero-pads to width 6& 10;// Result: "0x00fe"& 10; Floating-point values: & 10; & 10; & 10; Type & 10; Effect & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; a & 10; Hexadecimal-significand form (e.g. 1.8p+1 ). Lower-case digits and a lower-case p for the binary exponent. The flag adds a 0x prefix. & 10; & 10; & 10; A & 10; Same as a , but upper-case throughout. & 10; & 10; & 10; e & 10; Scientific notation with a lower-case e for the decimal exponent. & 10; & 10; & 10; E & 10; Scientific notation with an upper-case E . & 10; & 10; & 10; f & 10; Fixed-point notation. & 10; & 10; & 10; F & 10; Same as f , but renders nan as NAN and inf as INF . & 10; & 10; & 10; g & 10; General form: scientific notation when the exponent would be less than −4 or not less than the precision, otherwise fixed-point; trailing zeros are removed from the fractional part unless is set. A precision of 0 is interpreted as 1 . & 10; & 10; & 10; G & 10; Same as g , but uses E for the exponent and upper-case INF / NAN . & 10; & 10; & 10; none & 10; Shortest round-trip representation: the formatted value, when parsed back into the same floating-point type, reproduces the input bit for bit. & 10; & 10; & 10; Strings and characters: & 10; & 10; & 10; Type & 10; Effect & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; s & 10; Plain string output. Default for string types and for bool (which is rendered as true or false ). & 10; & 10; & 10; c & 10; Character output. Default for character types. Not allowed for bool . & 10; & 10; & 10; ? & 10; Debug output: the value is wrapped in single quotes (characters) or double quotes (strings), and non-printable, non-ASCII, and special characters are escaped using C-style escape sequences such as \n , \t , \" , and \u{...} . & 10; & 10; & 10; none & 10; Same as s for strings and bool , and as c for characters. & 10; & 10; & 10; fmt::format("{}", "tab\there"); // Result contains a literal tab character.& 10;fmt::format("{:?}", "tab\there"); // Result: "\"tab\\there\""& 10; Pointers: & 10; & 10; & 10; Type & 10; Effect & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; p & 10; Hexadecimal address prefixed by 0x . Default for pointer types. & 10; & 10; & 10; none & 10; Same as p . & 10; & 10; & 10; A C string ( char or const char ) accepts both the string presentation types and p , so the same value can be formatted as either text or an address. Chrono Format Specification The format specification for chrono duration and time point types as well as std::tm has the following syntax: chrono_format_spec ::= [[ fill ] align ][ width ]["." precision ][chrono_specs]& 10;chrono_specs ::= conversion_spec & 10; chrono_specs (conversion_spec literal_char)& 10;conversion_spec ::= "%" [padding_modifier] [locale_modifier] chrono_type& 10;literal_char ::= <a character other than '{', '}' or '%'>& 10;padding_modifier ::= "-" " " "0"& 10;locale_modifier ::= "E" "O"& 10;chrono_type ::= "a" "A" "b" "B" "c" "C" "d" "D" "e" & 10; "F" "g" "G" "h" "H" "I" "j" "m" "M" & 10; "n" "p" "q" "Q" "r" "R" "S" "t" "T" & 10; "u" "U" "V" "w" "W" "x" "X" "y" "Y" & 10; "z" "Z" "%" & 10; Literal chars are copied unchanged to the output. Precision is valid only for std::chrono::duration types with a floating-point representation type. The available presentation types ( chrono_type ) are: & 10; & 10; Type & 10; Meaning & 10; & 10; & 10; 'a' & 10; & 10; The abbreviated weekday name, e.g. "Sat". If the value does not contain a& 10; valid weekday, an exception of type format_error is thrown.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'A' & 10; & 10; The full weekday name, e.g. "Saturday". If the value does not contain a& 10; valid weekday, an exception of type format_error is thrown.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'b' & 10; & 10; The abbreviated month name, e.g. "Nov". If the value does not contain a& 10; valid month, an exception of type format_error is thrown.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'B' & 10; & 10; The full month name, e.g. "November". If the value does not contain a valid& 10; month, an exception of type format_error is thrown.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'c' & 10; & 10; The date and time representation, e.g. "Sat Nov 12 22:04:00 1955". The& 10; modified command %Ec produces the locale's alternate date and& 10; time representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'C' & 10; & 10; The year divided by 100 using floored division, e.g. "19". If the result& 10; is a single decimal digit, it is prefixed with 0. The modified command& 10; %EC produces the locale's alternative representation of the& 10; century.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'd' & 10; & 10; The day of month as a decimal number. If the result is a single decimal& 10; digit, it is prefixed with 0. The modified command %Od & 10; produces the locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'D' & 10; Equivalent to %m/%d/%y , e.g. "11/12/55". & 10; & 10; & 10; 'e' & 10; & 10; The day of month as a decimal number. If the result is a single decimal& 10; digit, it is prefixed with a space. The modified command %Oe & 10; produces the locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'F' & 10; Equivalent to %Y-%m-%d , e.g. "1955-11-12". & 10; & 10; & 10; 'g' & 10; & 10; The last two decimal digits of the ISO week-based year. If the result is a& 10; single digit it is prefixed by 0.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'G' & 10; & 10; The ISO week-based year as a decimal number. If the result is less than& 10; four digits it is left-padded with 0 to four digits.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'h' & 10; Equivalent to %b , e.g. "Nov". & 10; & 10; & 10; 'H' & 10; & 10; The hour (24-hour clock) as a decimal number. If the result is a single& 10; digit, it is prefixed with 0. The modified command %OH & 10; produces the locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'I' & 10; & 10; The hour (12-hour clock) as a decimal number. If the result is a single& 10; digit, it is prefixed with 0. The modified command %OI & 10; produces the locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'j' & 10; & 10; If the type being formatted is a specialization of duration, the decimal& 10; number of days without padding. Otherwise, the day of the year as a decimal& 10; number. Jan 1 is 001. If the result is less than three digits, it is& 10; left-padded with 0 to three digits.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'm' & 10; & 10; The month as a decimal number. Jan is 01. If the result is a single digit,& 10; it is prefixed with 0. The modified command %Om produces the& 10; locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'M' & 10; & 10; The minute as a decimal number. If the result is a single digit, it& 10; is prefixed with 0. The modified command %OM produces the& 10; locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'n' & 10; A new-line character. & 10; & 10; & 10; 'p' & 10; The AM/PM designations associated with a 12-hour clock. & 10; & 10; & 10; 'q' & 10; The duration's unit suffix. & 10; & 10; & 10; 'Q' & 10; & 10; The duration's numeric value (as if extracted via .count() ).& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'r' & 10; The 12-hour clock time, e.g. "10:04:00 PM". & 10; & 10; & 10; 'R' & 10; Equivalent to %H:%M , e.g. "22:04". & 10; & 10; & 10; 'S' & 10; & 10; Seconds as a decimal number. If the number of seconds is less than 10, the& 10; result is prefixed with 0. If the precision of the input cannot be exactly& 10; represented with seconds, then the format is a decimal floating-point number& 10; with a fixed format and a precision matching that of the precision of the& 10; input (or to a microseconds precision if the conversion to floating-point& 10; decimal seconds cannot be made within 18 fractional digits). The modified& 10; command %OS produces the locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 't' & 10; A horizontal-tab character. & 10; & 10; & 10; 'T' & 10; Equivalent to %H:%M:%S . & 10; & 10; & 10; 'u' & 10; & 10; The ISO weekday as a decimal number (1-7), where Monday is 1. The modified& 10; command %Ou produces the locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'U' & 10; & 10; The week number of the year as a decimal number. The first Sunday of the& 10; year is the first day of week 01. Days of the same year prior to that are& 10; in week 00. If the result is a single digit, it is prefixed with 0.& 10; The modified command %OU produces the locale's alternative& 10; representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'V' & 10; & 10; The ISO week-based week number as a decimal number. If the result is a& 10; single digit, it is prefixed with 0. The modified command %OV & 10; produces the locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'w' & 10; & 10; The weekday as a decimal number (0-6), where Sunday is 0. The modified& 10; command %Ow produces the locale's alternative representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'W' & 10; & 10; The week number of the year as a decimal number. The first Monday of the& 10; year is the first day of week 01. Days of the same year prior to that are& 10; in week 00. If the result is a single digit, it is prefixed with 0.& 10; The modified command %OW produces the locale's alternative& 10; representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'x' & 10; & 10; The date representation, e.g. "11/12/55". The modified command& 10; %Ex produces the locale's alternate date representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'X' & 10; & 10; The time representation, e.g. "10:04:00". The modified command& 10; %EX produces the locale's alternate time representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'y' & 10; & 10; The last two decimal digits of the year. If the result is a single digit& 10; it is prefixed by 0. The modified command %Oy produces the& 10; locale's alternative representation. The modified command %Ey & 10; produces the locale's alternative representation of offset from& 10; %EC (year only).& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'Y' & 10; & 10; The year as a decimal number. If the result is less than four digits it is& 10; left-padded with 0 to four digits. The modified command %EY & 10; produces the locale's alternative full year representation.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'z' & 10; & 10; The offset from UTC in the ISO 8601:2004 format. For example -0430 refers& 10; to 4 hours 30 minutes behind UTC. If the offset is zero, +0000 is used.& 10; The modified commands %Ez and %Oz insert a& 10; : between the hours and minutes: -04:30. If the offset& 10; information is not available, an exception of type& 10; format_error is thrown.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; 'Z' & 10; & 10; The time zone abbreviation. If the time zone abbreviation is not available,& 10; an exception of type format_error is thrown.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; '%' & 10; A % character. & 10; & 10; Specifiers that have a calendaric component such as 'd' (the day of month) are valid only for std::tm and time points but not durations. The available padding modifiers ( padding_modifier ) are: & 10; & 10; & 10; Type & 10; Meaning & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; ' ' & 10; Pad a numeric result with spaces. & 10; & 10; & 10; '-' & 10; Do not pad a numeric result string. & 10; & 10; & 10; '0' & 10; Pad a numeric result string with zeros. & 10; & 10; & 10; These modifiers are only supported for the 'H' , 'I' , 'M' , 'S' , 'U' , 'V' , 'W' , 'Y' , 'd' , 'j' and 'm' presentation types. Example: include <fmt/chrono.h>& 10;& 10;auto t = std::tm();& 10;t.tm_year = 2010 - 1900;& 10;t.tm_mon = 7;& 10;t.tm_mday = 4;& 10;t.tm_hour = 12;& 10;t.tm_min = 15;& 10;t.tm_sec = 58;& 10;fmt::print("{:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}", t);& 10;// Prints: 2010-08-04 12:15:58& 10; Range Format Specification The format specification for range types has the following syntax: range_format_spec ::= ["n"][range_type][":" range_underlying_spec] & 10; The 'n' option formats the range without the opening and closing brackets. The available presentation types for range_type are: & 10; & 10; & 10; Type & 10; Meaning & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; none & 10; Default format. & 10; & 10; & 10; 's' & 10; String format. The range is formatted as a string. & 10; & 10; & 10; '?⁠s' & 10; Debug format. The range is formatted as an escaped string. & 10; & 10; & 10; If range_type is 's' or '?s' , the range element type must be a character type. The 'n' option and range_underlying_spec are mutually exclusive with 's' and '?s' . The range_underlying_spec is parsed based on the formatter of the range's element type. By default, a range of characters or strings is printed escaped and quoted. But if any range_underlying_spec is provided (even if it is empty), then the characters or strings are printed according to the provided specification. Examples: fmt::print("{}", std::vector{10, 20, 30});& 10;// Output: [10, 20, 30]& 10;fmt::print("{:: x}", std::vector{10, 20, 30});& 10;// Output: [0xa, 0x14, 0x1e]& 10;fmt::print("{}", std::vector{'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'});& 10;// Output: ['h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o']& 10;fmt::print("{:n}", std::vector{'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'});& 10;// Output: 'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'& 10;fmt::print("{:s}", std::vector{'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'});& 10;// Output: "hello"& 10;fmt::print("{:?s}", std::vector{'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o', '\n'});& 10;// Output: "hello\n"& 10;fmt::print("{::}", std::vector{'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'});& 10;// Output: [h, e, l, l, o]& 10;fmt::print("{::d}", std::vector{'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'});& 10;// Output: [104, 101, 108, 108, 111]& 10;fmt::print("{:n:f}", std::array{std::numbers::pi, std::numbers::e});& 10;// Output: 3.141593, 2.718282& 10; A Combined Example The example below ties together several elements introduced above — nested replacement fields, fill characters, and centering — to draw a fixed-width box around a message: fmt::print(& 10; "┌{0:─^{2}}┐\n"& 10; "│{1: ^{2}}│\n"& 10; "└{0:─^{2}}┘\n", "", "Hello, world!", 20);& 10; Output: ┌────────────────────┐& 10;│ Hello, world! │& 10;└────────────────────┘& 10;
